audience: Engineers who know APIs and databases and need practical system-design reasoning about caches. Answers should explain what happens, who does the work, and what can go wrong in plain English.
prerequisites: An API handler can read and write records in a database.
Several application instances can handle requests at the same time.
Latency is the time a request takes; a system has limited processing capacity.
A database commit makes a completed write available to subsequent database reads in these scenarios.

slides.title: Stop repeating the same product lookup
paragraphs: A popular product page keeps asking the API for the same name, description, and price. Each request repeats a database lookup.

paragraphs.label: Cache
paragraphs.text: Keeps a reusable copy of a result. Reading that copy can save database work and shorten the wait for the page.

paragraphs: In this example, the database owns the product record. Losing the cached copy must not lose the product.
slides.remember: First identify repeated work that is worth avoiding. A cache adds another copy to manage.

slides.title: The same request can take two paths

paragraphs.label: Cache hit
paragraphs.text: The API finds product:42 in the cache and returns its stored details.

paragraphs.label: Cache miss
paragraphs.text: The entry is absent. The API reads the database, stores a copy in the cache, and returns the details.

paragraphs: A hit can still return an old price. Finding a value does not prove it matches the database.
slides.remember: A hit avoids this database lookup. A miss still needs the database.

slides.title: The application manages the cached copy

paragraphs.label: Cache-aside
paragraphs.text: The API checks and fills the cache explicitly. The cache does not fetch the product from the database on its own.

paragraphs.label: Cache key
paragraphs.text: Identifies the result to reuse. product:42 works for shared product details; prices in different currencies need distinct keys, such as product:42:USD.

paragraphs: Include the inputs that change the answer. Reusing one person's private result for another person is a data leak.
slides.remember: Define what the key identifies, who fills it, and where the authoritative data lives.

slides.title: The price changed. What does the next reader see?
paragraphs: A seller changes the price from $20 to $25. The cached $20 is now stale.

paragraphs.label: Invalidation
paragraphs.text: Remove the cached entry after saving the new price in the database. A later miss reloads it.

paragraphs: These steps are not atomic. Removal can fail, or an overlapping read can put an older value back after removal.
slides.remember: Invalidation alone does not guarantee freshness. For checkout, validate the price against the authoritative data as part of accepting the order.

slides.title: An entry can disappear for different reasons

paragraphs.label: Time to live, or TTL
paragraphs.text: Sets how long an entry may remain before it expires. A 60-second TTL does not refresh the product every minute; a later miss must load it again.

paragraphs.label: Eviction
paragraphs.text: Removes entries to make room. A least-recently-used policy favors removing entries that have not been read recently.

paragraphs: A product can be evicted before its TTL ends. Some configurations reject new entries when full instead of evicting existing ones.
slides.remember: TTL limits an entry's lifetime, not the age of the source data used to fill it.

slides.title: Two API servers can hold different prices

paragraphs.label: Local cache
paragraphs.text: Lives inside each API process. Reads avoid a network call, but each process fills and updates its own copy. One can hold $20 while another holds $25.

paragraphs.label: Shared cache
paragraphs.text: Several API servers use a separate cache service, such as Redis or Memcached. They can reuse entries, but each lookup adds a network call and the service needs operating.

slides.remember: Sharing reduces separate copies. It does not automatically keep the cache current with the database.

slides.title: A missing popular product can flood the database

paragraphs.label: Cache stampede
paragraphs.text: Many requests miss the same product together and repeat its database lookup. Coalescing requests lets concurrent readers share one in-progress lookup.

paragraphs: A cache outage can turn most reads into database traffic. Limit fallback work to what the database can handle; reject excess requests or serve older data only where the product rules permit it.
Test with an empty or unavailable cache. A warm cache can hide insufficient database capacity.
slides.remember: Falling back to the database is a load decision, not a free recovery path.

slides.title: Explain what you would cache and why
paragraphs: For our product page, propose caching frequently read descriptions that tolerate a brief delay after edits. Keep checkout price validation tied to the order's authoritative data.

paragraphs.label: Measure
paragraphs.text: Compare response time and database load before and after caching. Track the fraction of lookups that hit, and what happens during misses.

paragraphs: If requests rarely reuse results, or freshness is too hard to maintain, the cache may cost more than it saves.
slides.remember: Name the cached result, its key, acceptable staleness, update policy, and failure behavior.

questions.question: A travel API returns a station guide for a station ID and a requested language. English and Spanish guides differ. The database takes 80 ms to build a guide; a cache lookup takes 2 ms. The same few station-language pairs account for most reads, and guides change only weekly. The application uses cache-aside, and the database remains the source of truth. Explain why caching could help, propose a cache key, and walk through both a hit and a miss. Identify who reads the database and who stores the cached result. You do not need to calculate an average latency.

A library API caches opening hours under one key. Its cache-aside reader fetches a database value on a miss and later stores that fetched value. Its writer commits new database hours and then deletes the cache key. Consider this exact order, with no other operations: 1. Reader A misses the cache and reads the old hours from the database, then pauses before filling the cache. 2. Writer B commits the new hours. 3. Writer B deletes the cache key. 4. Reader A resumes and stores the old hours it already fetched. 5. Reader C looks up the key before it expires. Which hours does C receive, why did deletion fail to prevent that, and can the team claim that every read after B finishes sees the new hours? If this endpoint must always show the latest committed hours, name a simple way to avoid serving this stale cached copy; you do not need to design a concurrency protocol.

A weather API stores the current forecast at 12:00 with a TTL of ten minutes. There is no background refresh, no write-triggered invalidation, and no serving expired entries. The source forecast changes at 12:02. In case A, the entry stays in memory until it expires; requests arrive at 12:03 and 12:11. In case B, the cache removes the entry at 12:04 to free memory, and the next request arrives at 12:05. For each request, explain whether it can use the original cached forecast or must fetch the source. Explain what the ten-minute TTL promises, what it does not promise, and why the memory removal is a different event.

An event API runs on four application instances. Each currently has its own in-memory cache of the same room map. Any instance can handle the next request. When an organizer changes the map, the database updates and only the instance handling that write deletes its local copy. The team wants one cache deletion to remove the cached map used by every instance. It can accept a 2 ms network lookup. Compare keeping these independent local caches with moving the map to one shared cache. Choose the simpler fit for this specific goal, explain what happens to requests sent to the other instances today, and name one cost or failure consequence of your choice. Assume a single shared cache entry and no concurrent cache fills for this question.

A tournament schedule endpoint receives 10,000 requests per second, mostly for the same schedule. The database can safely handle only 500 schedule reads per second. The cache normally absorbs almost all reads. First, the popular key expires while many requests arrive together. Second, consider a separate incident where the entire cache is unreachable for a minute. The product permits returning the last known schedule for up to 60 seconds, and it permits a temporary error if necessary to protect the database. Explain how each incident threatens the database. Propose one concrete way to reduce duplicate database reads after the single-key expiration, and describe an outage response that does not send every request straight to the database. Explain how your response reduces work; naming a technique alone is insufficient.

An internal inspection service stores a result for each newly completed inspection. Every result has a unique ID, and each result is retrieved exactly once before archival. A database read takes 2 ms. The endpoint has a 100 ms latency budget and receives ten reads per second; the database can comfortably handle 1,000 reads per second. There is no other reader of these results. A teammate proposes filling a cache after every database read so future requests can reuse the result. Should the team add this cache now? Explain the expected benefit and costs, and name a change in the workload that would make you reconsider.
